query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a ductilizing element such as niobium (Nb) to the HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy will improve its ductility and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy composed solely of group IV elements, which exhibits intrinsic brittleness and limited plasticity.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount of Nb to form a quaternary (or multicomponent) alloy, e.g. HfZrTiNb.
generation.conditions: Standard mechanical testing conditions at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures, under conventional processing and loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a more ductile solid solution phase (likely with an improved body‐centered cubic structure) that facilitates enhanced dislocation movement and activates additional deformation mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Nb is expected to increase atomic size misfit and modify the local bonding environment. This promotes multiple deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation slip and twinning) and reduces the intrinsic brittleness of the phase, thereby enhancing overall ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-modified HfZrTi alloy will exhibit increased plastic strain to failure and improved fracture toughness while maintaining high strength compared to the original HfZrTi alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified HfZrTi HEA, which shows lower ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected as long as the Nb content is optimized to avoid excessive formation of brittle intermetallic compounds or secondary phases. The overall composition must remain within the refractory HEA regime.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb concentration and exact magnitude of ductility/toughness improvement remain uncertain until validated by targeted experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: the baseline HfZrTi HEA and a modified version with added Nb (e.g., HfZrTiNb). Conduct tensile and fracture toughness tests under identical conditions and perform microstructural characterization (using XRD and electron microscopy) to identify phase changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-containing alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in plasticity (elongation) and fracture toughness, or if it develops deleterious brittle phases compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
